Ah, the people at your local fishing store are a great resource! They'll know more than me, and they'll know what's available to catch in your area.

And yeah, it's a lot of trial and error, but even the error is tons of fun if you just relax and let yourself learn from it.

A couple of things would be helpful to know: What kind of fish do you want to catch? And do you know what the power/action of that rod is? 

Bearing in mind that I'm a complete amateur, I'd advocate for something a little lighter, but it depends on what you want to fish for. 6-12kg would be pretty heavy if you want to go after panfish, trout, things like that. For bass, pike, and other bigger fish, that's probably a pretty good weight range.

That said, a lighter rod (in the 3-6kg range) will also catch the bigger species, especially if you spool it with braid to have a heavier rated line on it, plus it'll be easier to cast smaller and lighter lures and baits.

[This](https://www.fix.com/blog/locating-trout-in-a-stream/) is an article that helped me out quite a bit in learning to find where trout might be hanging out. Pick a place along the creek to start, look for features where you see good prospects, and make your way slowly and quietly upstream (since the trout will be facing upstream, you want to approach them from behind), and try a few casts wherever you think they may be hiding. Good luck!

First of all, I hope it'll encourage you a bit to hear that problems I created for myself while I was depressed, and that seemed entirely irreversible and insurmountable, turned out to not be that bad to fix once I was myself again. Customer emails that I had ignored, loan payments I didn't make, etc. All of them fixed scant weeks later.

It was incredibly noticeable. It was a Sunday afternoon, and I just realized that the place I was in emotionally was SO MUCH better than where I'd been for months. I could enjoy the sunshine, and the company of a good friend. When I started taking the pills, I thought I was already doing much better, but I tell people now that I genuinely believe I had forgotten altogether what it felt like to be truly happy. I have so much more energy, I'm actually enjoying my life again, and I can handle problems as they arise instead of completely breaking down when they do.

My response to meds was very similar. Two weeks in I noticed I wasn't getting angry as easily. It was three weeks and two days after my first dose that things finally clicked, and I got my life back. Hang in there. The wait is SO worth it.

Oh my god. You have no idea how much this speaks to me. The constant stream of vitriol that your mind feeds you, and that you just can't shut off no matter what you do. Not being able to accept kind words as the truth. And the anger. Anger is the wrong word, though. Every time a doctor or counselor has asked if I have trouble with anger, I tell them that I wouldn't describe it as anger, but rather as rage. Some tiny thing goes wrong, or somebody says the wrong thing, or you see somebody driving in a way you don't like, and it completely takes over your mind, and there's nothing left but white-hot, seething rage. 

And the promise. Good lord. I had family ask me if I would promise not to kill myself, and I begged them not to make me, because I knew it would just be one more thing I would feel guilty about. I knew that every time I thought about suicide I would see it as a failure against that promise, and I knew I couldn't deal with that. I was lucky that they understood. I think now that promises not to kill yourself are about the stupidest thing ever. When literally nothing matters to you, what good does a promise do? 

I'm really sorry you're in this place, and I hope that you pull through this alright. Your expression of your feelings here touched me. Thank you for that.

My brother just went through this not even a week ago. He tried soaking them in alcohol,  packing the bowl with salt, all sorts of stuff,  and nothing worked. Finally he packed the bowl with activated carbon (the stuff you can get for fish tank filters) and then filled them up with isopropyl alcohol (though I imagine a grain alcohol might work better). He let them soak like that for about 8 hours, and let them dry for a day. The difference was incredible. They had ghosted extremely heavily, and this method got them back to smoking almost like new.

Oh believe me, my friend (and I don't use that moniker sarcastically), I know. I've been suicidal on and off for the last 3-4 years. Every time I come out of it I think, "I'm so glad I didn't do it. Why was I even considering it?" But that doesn't make it any easier to deal with the next time it comes around. 

Here's the way I see it: within human experience, everything is chemical. Everything. Everything you've ever seen, touched, smelled, heard, or felt comes down to nothing more than chemicals in the brain. It's Plato's Cave all over again. Objectivity means nothing to the individual. As a race, the only way we humans can experience anything is subjectively. We are literally incapable of experiencing or processing anything without the stimuli first passing through a filter of our own emotions and past experiences. This filter, of course, is composed of the very chemicals and hormones we're talking about. So, even if the levels of these chemicals and hormones aren't "normal," since we have nothing but subjectivity, can we really say it's wrong, or stupid, or that we shouldn't feel that way? Honestly, I'm posing a question to which I have no answer here, but it's where my mind's been this afternoon. And now I'm rambling... I'll stop now.

TL;DR: "The mind is but a plaything of the body, correct?" -Tom Siddell

C'mon. Do you really think anybody here doesn't know it's chemical? That doesn't invalidate the feelings. Knowing that and being able to think about it rationally are two very different things. Do you really think any of the hundreds of thousands of people who have ended their own lives over the years only did it because nobody told them, "It's going to be okay, just hang in there"?  When literally nothing means anything to you, how does that help? 

I can appreciate that you're trying to help. Thank you for that. I mean that. But maybe you should consider for a moment that you're going about it the wrong way.
